Chapter Two: Understanding the Impact of Control and the Illusion of Responsibility
Now that you’ve started to spot codependency patterns, let’s take a closer look at something that often shows up right alongside them—control. Have you ever felt like it’s your job to manage how others feel, what they decide, or even how things turn out for people around you? If so, you’re not alone. For a lot of us, this belief creeps in quietly, and before we know it, we’re carrying the weight of everyone else’s world on our shoulders. On the surface, trying to control things can actually feel pretty comforting. It gives you a sense of purpose, like you’re holding things together. But over time, it can also be completely draining. It’s that feeling of being stretched too thin—always stepping in, always trying to keep the peace. Control in codependent relationships can show up in all sorts of ways. Sometimes, it’s really obvious—maybe you’re the one always giving advice, making decisions for someone else, or solving problems before they even happen. Other times, it’s more subtle. Maybe you find yourself watching for changes in someone’s mood, anticipating what they’ll need next, or even changing how you act just to keep things calm. The hidden message? If you just try hard enough, you can keep disaster away and make sure everyone’s okay. But why do we do this? For many people, the urge to control is rooted in fear. If you grew up in a home that felt unpredictable or even chaotic, control might’ve felt like the only way to stay safe. If you could manage a parent’s anger or drinking, maybe the family wouldn’t fall apart. If you met everyone’s needs, perhaps you’d finally get the love or approval you were looking for. Over time, these habits turn into automatic ways of relating—even in adulthood. Here’s something important to remember: control is really just an illusion. No matter how hard you try, you can’t actually manage someone else’s feelings, choices, or recovery. And the more you pour your energy into fixing others, the less you have left for yourself. This usually leads to frustration, resentment, and that sinking feeling of never being enough. Imagine a lifeguard leaping into the water to save someone who isn’t actually drowning. But instead of helping, they both end up struggling to stay afloat. That’s what it’s like in a codependent relationship when the urge to rescue takes over—your own well-being is at risk, and neither person really gets what they need. Now, letting go of control doesn’t mean you stop caring or turn your back on people you love. It’s about recognizing what’s truly yours to carry—and what isn’t. It’s allowing others to face the real consequences of their choices, even when that’s tough to watch. In a way, it’s a form of respect. You’re saying, “I trust that you’re capable of handling your own life.” So, how do you start to release control? Here are a few steps you might try:
- Notice when you feel the urge to jump in, and give yourself a moment to pause. - Ask yourself, “Is this really my problem to solve, or does it belong to someone else?” - Let others experience the results of their own decisions, without rushing in to rescue or enable. - And most importantly, bring your focus back to your own feelings and needs, instead of trying to manage everyone else’s.
Of course, this isn’t easy. You might notice anxiety, guilt, or even a sense of helplessness creeping in. And it’s totally normal to worry that if you stop controlling, everything will fall apart. But the truth is, letting go creates space—for you, and for the people you care about—to grow. Over time, you can shift from a focus on control to one of self-care and personal empowerment. That doesn’t mean ignoring the needs of others, but approaching your relationships from a place of wholeness instead of fear. It’s kind of like tending your own garden, trusting that others will do the same. So, here’s the key takeaway: It’s okay to let go. When you do, you open the door for healthier, more balanced connections—and you finally get to reclaim your own energy and peace of mind.
